For a spectral input, a random surface profile is generated first subdividing the spectrum into discrete frequency bands. An AIRY wave with a random phase angle is then generated for each frequency band. The Wave Response program then reproduces the surface profile by the linear addition of AIRY waves.

The total wave kinematics are determined by adding the velocities and accelerations from the various components.

![](SACS2024_SACS_Documentation/chunk37_b1241a95965f830e5c6ee7c581d19dd3b747d0b3af990efba91e6a225c2807ac.jpg)

When a wave spectrum is specified, the spectrum itself is analyzed and broken into Airy wave components. Only wave components with periods that are divisible into the analysis time duration are considered as possible components.

The period of a possible wave component n, is determined from the following equation:

$$T_{n} = \frac{T_{D}}{n} \quad n = 1, 2, 3 \dots n_{\max }$$

The input spectrum is divided into strips with each strip having a center frequency corresponding to the frequency of one of the possible wave components.

![](SACS2024_SACS_Documentation/chunk37_1fc8374c851220d215a51a59eab6286ea7d35d5591ad2a0eb394c55cc96582e5.jpg)

3.1.3 Multiple Random Seeds

By default, one seed is used when generating the random phase angles of the wave components. A set of sequential equally spaced seeds or a set of user input seeds can be used to generate numerous random surfaces of the random wave.

3.1.4 Equally Spaced Seeds

Numerous equally spaced sequential seeds can be used by specifying the number of seeds and the first seed value on the WSPEC input line. A detailed description of this input line can be found in the Wave Response manual.

![](SACS2024_SACS_Documentation/chunk37_4564ad5377875f5a5d8cf76f65098d3a5f34cfced2f261bafee4c21ce711f418.jpg)

The above input defines 20 random surfaces with an initial seed of 10. Seeds generated: 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, … 29

3.1.5 Hydrodynamic Properties

Hydrodynamic properties generated automatically using a dummy reference wave selected to wet the maximum height likely during the random wave analysis (also used to determine the number of load segments per member for an accurate representation of loading). The wave direction should be the same as the random wave and the crest position located at the center of the structure.

3.1.6 Aerodynamic Properties

If random wind is included in the random wave analysis, aerodynamic and a reference wind must be specified in the Seastate input or SACS model file. Reference wind load data is specified in the same load case as the reference wave. The wind direction and mean wind velocity should be input in the reference wind.

3.1.7 User Defined Seeds

Up to 99 seeds used to generate surface profiles can be specified.

The number of seeds is designated in columns 6-7 on the WSPEC line. The seeds to be used to generate the surface profiles are input on the RNSEED line. A detailed description of the input lines can be found in the Wave Response manual.

The following designates that 15 user defined seeds are to be used to generate random wave surface profiles.

![](SACS2024_SACS_Documentation/chunk37_35ed2e1d11676f1e19380b6c87a840e3fdd88f947f51c7876a2e7e8fd22ea071.jpg)

3.1.8 Transient Reduction

The initial transient from a wave response time history analysis can be ignored by the use of the transient reduction option 'TR' in columns 61-62 of the THIST input line. This option ignores the first 10 seconds of the wave response time history analysis results.

![](SACS2024_SACS_Documentation/chunk37_f5c02b5c74a3929ef4c34fc991af09a78dc4c5dd6b29af7f0506e173d5a6353f.jpg)

3.1.9 Wind Loading on Turbine

The wind loading on the turbine causes the rotation of the wind turbine, which in turn generates aerodynamic and mechanical forces on the top of the tower, which can be represented by a force time history.

![](SACS2024_SACS_Documentation/chunk37_e280d1c4e4c7d35031bd3a029d745730a56776ca583de3d710f79a89f74e01bd.jpg)

A force time history can be input using the THLOAD header input line followed by the TIME and JLOD line describing the time input and joint force time history input respectively. A detailed description of these input lines can be found in the Wave Response manual.

The example below shows a typical force time history input file with the THLOAD input line describing the input units and a force factor, followed by the TIME line defining the input time increment value and the JLOD input line describing the joint name and the force/moment input values. The TIME and JLOD lines are repeated for all subsequent time increments.

3.1.10 Time History Analysis of Combined Seismic, Wave, and Wind Turbine Loads

SACS Wave Response program can perform a combined analysis of wave loads, wind turbine forces, and seismic loads in the time-history simulation (i.e., 'TH' or 'TG' is selected in columns 68-69 on the WROPT line). THLOAD input line can be utilized to import up to two (2) time-history files containing wind turbine forces and seismic forces (or any other force time-history files). Once the THLOAD lines are entered in the Wave Response input file, the files can be selected in SACS Analysis Generator.

SACS Dynamic Response program can automatically generate the base-driven earthquake forces by selecting the 'WVR' option on THLOAD in the Dynamic Response Input file. The users are referred to the Dynamic Response user manual for additional information. Input files for other force time-history types can be manually created through SACS Datagen and by selecting the Force Time History Input File - Wave Response input type.

The following example illustrates the inputs for two force time-history files. The first input is the Wind Turbine forces given in Flex 5 format, while the second file contains base-driven earthquake load in SACS format.

```c
1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 123456789012345678901234567890123456789012345678901234567890  
1 \*First Time-History File  
2 THLOAD MN FNT05  
3 \*Second Time-History File  
# 4 THLOAD MN
```

Consider the following notes about importing the time-history files:

1. If the Wave Response Analysis Time Increment (entered on the WAVTIM line) does not match the time steps in the imported files, the imported forces will be linearly interpolated.   
2. If the time histories of the imported files are shorter than the Wave Response Analysis Time, the imported time history will be padded by the force values at the last time step.   
3. If the time histories of the imported files are longer than the Wave Response analysis time, the extra time steps will be ignored.   
4. If the imported history starts at the non-zero time, the imported time history will be padded by the force values at the first step between the time zero and the imported history starting time.5. The force time-history file types entered on THLOAD lines must conform to the file types selected in the SACS Analysis Generator. Otherwise, the Wave Response returns error messages.

## 3.2 SACS WIND TURBINE PROCESS

For an uncoupled analysis involving multiple time history simulations, the SACS Wind Turbine Process allows the user to automate the process for both fatigue and strength analysis as shown below:

3.2.1 Fatigue Analysis

![](SACS2024_SACS_Documentation/chunk37_2997e5116b7527bd4c1d8d6433abc8bf78b000ac4f45f48c1d7020212ba18098.jpg)

The above analysis process requires a user generated control file and a partial fatigue input file. The automated process allows parallel processing through a multi core functionality to reduce the run time for multiple time history simulations.

The control file as shown below contains the following information:



| Flag F indicating a fatigue analysis |
| --- |
| Directory location for wave response input file for a given simulation |
| Name of the Wave Response generated loads common solution file for the jacket structure |
| Name of the Wave Response generated loads common solution file for the foundation |
| A group name for damage summation |
| Occurrence data for this simulation |
| The name of the Wave Response time history run file a particular simulation |
| Repeat the above (minus the flag) for other simulations. |



The example below shows a typical control file for six simulations.

```txt
FLAG F  
DIRECTORY C:\work\paris 2013\ uncoupled wind turbine fatigue analysis\1  
CSF psicsf.xxx  
PCSF pilcsf.xxx  
WVRRUN wvrxxx.runx  
GROUP 1  
VAR 40000  
DIRECTORY C:\work\paris 2013\ uncoupled wind turbine fatigue analysis\2  
CSF psicsf.xxx  
PCSF pilcsf.xxx  
WVRRUN wvrxxx.runx  
GROUP 2  
VAR 402234  
DIRECTORY C:\work\paris 2013\ uncoupled wind turbine fatigue analysis\3  
CSF psicsf.xxx  
PCSF pilcsf.xxx  
WVRRUN wvrxxx.runx  
GROUP 1  
VAR 10330  
DIRECTORY C:\work\paris 2013\ uncoupled wind turbine fatigue analysis\4  
CSF psicsf.xxx  
PCSF pilcsf.xxx  
WVRRUN wvrxxx.runx  
GROUP 2  
VAR 4022  
DIRECTORY C:\work\paris 2013\ uncoupled wind turbine fatigue analysis\5  
CSF psicsf.xxx  
PCSF pilcsf.xxx  
WVRRUN wvrxxx.runx  
GROUP 1  
VAR 400000  
DIRECTORY C:\work\paris 2013\ uncoupled wind turbine fatigue analysis\6  
CSF psicsf.xxx  
PCSF pilcsf.xxx  
WVRRUN wvrxxx.runx  
GROUP 2  
VAR 400000 
```

The partial fatigue input file contains information on the fatigue design life, the fatigue time period over which the occurrence data is measured, the choice of SCF's and SN curves in addition to any overrides. The fatigue load cases are automatically generated by SACS using the information provided in the control file.

The example below shows a typical partial fatigue input file:

```txt
TITLEWIND POWER GENERATION FATIGUE ANALYSIS  
* Fatigue design life is 20 years  
* Cycles based on 1 year time period  
* Safety factor is 2.0  
* API X-Prime S-N curve  
* SCF's by Efthymiou  
* Inline SCF's in accordance to  
FTOPTG 20. 1. 2.0 SMAXP SK 5 LPEFT  
FTOPT2 PTPTVC DN2 TI5 O  
*TOPT3 P  
SCFLM 6.0 1.5  
* Remove jacket joints that are not tubular connections  
JNTSEL RM 401L 403L 405L 1 3 5 1014 501P 503P 505P  
* Sleeve end joints  
JNTSEL RM SL01 SL03 SL11 SL13 SL31 SL33  
*  
JNTSEL RM 11 13 15 31 33 35 
```

The example below shows a typical fatigue input file after the fatigue load case has been generated by SACS:

```txt
TITLEWIND POWER GENERATION FATIGUE ANALYSIS  
* fatigue life is 20 years  
* Cycles based on 1 year time period  
* Safety factor is 2.0  
FTOPTG 20. 1. 2.0 SMAXP SK 5 LPEFT  
FTOPT2 PTPTVC 3.0 -3.0AWS TI5 O  
FTOPT3 P  
* Stress Time History duration is WVR analysis duration x number of random seeds  
* Stress Time History duration = 600 X 1 = 600 seconds  
* 1 year has 31,536,000 seconds  
* Number of stress cycles in 1 year is 31,536,000/600 = 52,560 cycles  
FTCASE 1400000.000 1.0 THS 1  
END 
```

The first step in the automated process involves the generation a SACS wave response common solution file.

The figure below shows the input files required by the SACS Wave Response module for a typical time history simulation to generate a SACS common solution file to be used for a subsequent fatigue analysis. In this example a wave surface profile along with a force time history input is used. A modal analysis of the structure is required using the SACS DYNPAC module to generate the mass and mode files. The reference seastate input file is required to generate the hydrodynamic and aerodynamic properties as discussed earlier.

![](SACS2024_SACS_Documentation/chunk37_33c7e94d3cdea62e7411fee4ff42412f44e57d26647130f4089ecb446754fc45.jpg)

After the generation of all wave response common solution files, the fatigue damage calculations are performed as shown below.

## 3.3 STRENGTH ANALYSIS

![](SACS2024_SACS_Documentation/chunk37_8ff3cdaf3a240a1ab73a64788360cad97eaa31d96ee59b6ac2fa841cd2bbcede.jpg)

The automated strength analysis procedure requires a user defined control file, a partial seastate input file in addition to a PSI and a joint can input files. The automated process allows the use of parallel processing through a multi core functionality to reduce the analysis run time. The numerous unity check results from multiple time history analysis are stored in a database which is subsequently filtered for critical conditions.

The control file contains the following information:



| Flag S indicating a strength analysis |
| --- |
| Directory location for wave response input file for a given simulation |
| Name of the OCI file containing the dynamic Wave Response generated loads |
| The name of the wave response run file for the time history analysis for a given simulation |
| A partial safety factor for gravity loads |
| A partial safety factor for environmental loads |
| A partial load factor for extreme turbine loads. |
| Repeat of the above information (minus the flag) for other simulations. |



The example below shows a typical control file for strength analysis.

![](SACS2024_SACS_Documentation/chunk37_55bff4ebbb0a9854205a52dfcef4d969d893520093504567fffffb8fb8d16bde.jpg)

The partial seastate input file contains a LCSEL load case select line containing the names of the default names of the Wave Response dynamic load cases, hydrodynamic modeling and all gravity load cases. The combinations required for the strength analysis containing the dynamic and gravity loads together with the safety factors will automatically be generated by SACS.

NOTE: The uncoupled strength analysis requires the MST option to be used on the Wave Response options line WROPT to generate six load cases corresponding to max/min base shear, max/min over turning moment and max/min torque on the structure. The generated load cases are automatically named A001 to A006.

The example below shows a typical partial seastate input file.

![](SACS2024_SACS_Documentation/chunk37_4e1d22e6c5f6380b99684fa78a1d296a551d485fb0173745237867bbfa30c894.jpg)

The example below shows the seastate file after the load combinations have been automatically generated by SACS.

## 3.4 STRENGTH ANALYSIS – CONSTRAINED WAVE

For extreme design load cases a constrained wave approach may be used to ensure the structure experiences a maximum height wave by embedding one non-linear regular wave with height Hmax into a series of irregular linear waves.

The New Wave theory used to describe non-linear regular wave surface profile.

Airy waves used to describe the irregular wave surface profile.

![](SACS2024_SACS_Documentation/chunk37_afd1cd9587ac48c5fb491531a7f2cb6d88f28f3780909d8258c24e8f0513dcf0.jpg)

The constrained wave is blended into the irregular surface over a region (insertion time – 3*Tp) and (insertion time + 3*Tp). Where Tp is the period of the constrained wave.

The insertion time, peak period and the maximum crest elevation are defined on the WVINS input line in the wave response input file as shown below:

![](SACS2024_SACS_Documentation/chunk37_59d4d31f27ea04c49a24c5301f8216c540a609a41b2d627d6c63dd1ed0fc1e34.jpg)

![](SACS2024_SACS_Documentation/chunk37_1415f17eca36146f7d93f2d0faf15f931501a8e59c60e9ad6f8252e9955a2297.jpg)

![](SACS2024_SACS_Documentation/chunk37_ebc480391e3f5435d1d7f6838237f0fa466d073624e0ab2b87b005bed0ba0be2.jpg)

Fatigue/Member Check/Joint Design in

The SACS interface to NREL's FAST aero-elastic program offers a fully integrated and a nonintegrated approach. For the integrated approach the source codes of Wave Response and FAST version 7.1 are combined and compiled into a single program. Here both analyses are coupled together by using SACS generated mode shapes and dynamic properties in the FAST analysis. For the non-integrated approach the two executables are treated as separate entities and are connected at an interface joint in the structure through displacement and rotational compatibility. The iterative check to ensure compatibility compliance is conducted in FAST.

## 4.1 SACS-FAST INTEGRATED ANALYSIS PROCEDURE

For a SACS-FAST Analysis, the SACS portion of the analysis is subjected to mainly wave loading and is analyzed using SACS while the FAST portion mainly analyses for wind turbine loads.

A general set up of the analysis is shown in the steps below:

The turbine loads are divided as shown below.

![](SACS2024_SACS_Documentation/chunk37_6f1d27a2525418c5c72f7e24d8a5572d61a570a2b46924fcb470134c06884f13.jpg)

The internal analysis procedure in the integrated approach is described the flow chart below.

![](SACS2024_SACS_Documentation/chunk37_118b88cb478aa0df485dacc706c0a2f2a719c338f19020d33fba831e2909e663.jpg)

The detailed analysis steps are as follows:

1. Conduct a modal analysis using SACS DYNPAC module to generate the mass and mode files.   
2. Generate a Wave Response input file as shown in the example below.

![](SACS2024_SACS_Documentation/chunk37_d138f942165028079d1fa969fff9c49d76ffd58398eeca6e8139cfbcbc3f143d.jpg)

Select the 'ALL' option on the Wave Response options input line, WROPT, to output loads for all time steps. Select the ES option to generate equivalent static loads and the WM option to generate generalized forces for the SACS-FAST analysis.

![](SACS2024_SACS_Documentation/chunk37_1786730037400c68d09182adab79ef5ffb297d18faa95feb778cfaf132f34ec9.jpg)

Reference all the nodes used to describe the tower model on the JTOWR input line. It is required that these joints are specified beginning at the tower bottom and in order of increasing elevation. The last joint is the hub joint.

![](SACS2024_SACS_Documentation/chunk37_2cea5e1437e2a0488ea393b023ce3273102dcd5741678ef4a554f3f0b4af8695.jpg)

Enter the analysis time and the analysis increment on the WAVTIM input line.

![](SACS2024_SACS_Documentation/chunk37_56d961fb7ce30e7b47e9660e95b9c778078d883e65068a26384e9f7c52233305.jpg)

Enter the number of integration time steps used per output time increment on the FAST input line.

![](SACS2024_SACS_Documentation/chunk37_c94f2e75d102d7aedc1b37ebb5d28af918f8a97514ee9c4aab358c117b58dc9f.jpg)

3. Set up the FAST analysis with all supporting and required input files. If the blade pitch and torque controller DLL file for NREL 5MW wind turbine (DISCON.DLL) is to be used. The appropriate option should be selected in the FAST input files and proper values should be entered in “BladedDLLParameters.dat” file. This file should be placed in the same directory as the FAST files. Sample “BladedDLLParameters.dat” can be found in the SACS system directory.   
4. Run the SACS-FAST Integrated analysis to generate an OCI file containing the structural model and the generated equivalent static loads. The OCI file can subsequently be used for fatigue or strength analysis.

The overall analysis procedure for Fatigue/Strength involving the SACS-FAST interface is depicted in the workflow below.

![](SACS2024_SACS_Documentation/chunk37_a961446f13a4fd84807a1cc25518bbf2f290c2c8383d9be47e9f6af1ac6de74f.jpg)

The general analysis procedure for pile linearization (generation of a pile super element) is outlined below. Please refer to the SACS PSI manual for detailed guidance on the generation of a pile super element.

![](SACS2024_SACS_Documentation/chunk37_2223949c7edbf1dc6bd94f559ae4f53ec7b3174288a1042a7dc450a8f330ad8c.jpg)

The procedure for a modal analysis is shown in the workflow below. Please refer to the SACS DYNPAC manual for detailed guidance on input to DYNPAC.

![](SACS2024_SACS_Documentation/chunk37_b9b5ff5ddbbd8213c5fa8d789d054e88b2a785b7410da2dce62ca3e796d8a2b9.jpg)

Using the files generated above, as SACS-FAST analysis is then performed to generate a SACS OCI file for each simulation. The output OCI file contains the model definition and the generated inertial load cases. The workflow below shows a typical SACS-FAST analysis for the nth simulation.

![](SACS2024_SACS_Documentation/chunk37_d78944ecb559ad7c6aca80e8731f1b5f1a8dda075ca594b95d5f5a7b148e261d.jpg)

For a fatigue analysis the loads are generated for all time points as shown in the wave response input file below.

![](SACS2024_SACS_Documentation/chunk37_609b6f996e51d8f6f7770d88d9ded1a12a36c8c5fff1f1988c6731789444838e.jpg)

For a strength analysis six load cases are generated corresponding to max/min overturning moment, base shear and torque using the MST wave response option as shown below.

![](SACS2024_SACS_Documentation/chunk37_e75e3b2cf5b6ed269432dd97c5658adcfb3ccab6ba64cb5031c7260c19d98853.jpg)

4.1.1 Fatigue Analysis

For a fatigue analysis, the OCI files are used as the SACS model input files to conduct a static analysis for each simulation and output a SACS common solution file. This procedure is repeated for all simulations resulting in an equal number of common solution files.

![](SACS2024_SACS_Documentation/chunk37_4297fb075f2cff17695215d81d6ecda4b922264d17cabc87a22f00b6cde5f03c.jpg)

A time history fatigue analysis is then preformed for each simulation using a fatigue input file and the SACS common solution file. The damage from all simulations are summed to obtain the total damage.

![](SACS2024_SACS_Documentation/chunk37_5b2654689bdfae4fd3c5c2ef1901cb3596ce4ee78c3e78bde317b4fa828025a9.jpg)

4.1.2 Strength Analysis

For a strength analysis a static analysis is preformed using the output OCI file from the SACS-FAST analysis for each simulation together with a seastate input file as shown below:

![](SACS2024_SACS_Documentation/chunk37_ae8023f33f8854a1d36e288de8cf9fbf189cbc579116ee21e6f416f823863b20.jpg)

The seastate input file contains all structural dead loads and combinations as shown below.

![](SACS2024_SACS_Documentation/chunk37_ff51531b8d8eeb3eb70e02a3066320113ad3a0e0e2c3d132932e5e7517a7294c.jpg)

## 4.2 SACS-FAST NON-INTEGRATED ANALYSIS PROCEDURE

The SACS-FAST Non-Integrated analysis workflow for a Fatigue or a Strength analysis is the same as that for the integrated approach. However, the SACS-FAST analysis process is different and is outlined below:

4.2.1 FAST version 7.xx and older

1. Setup the wave response input file with wave and wind loading applied to the structure.

Enter “WM” in columns 68-69 of the WROPT line

Insert the JTOWR line.

Note: In JTOWR line – only mention ONE joint name. This should be the interface joint.

2. Setup FAST analysis with all supporting and required files.

Note1: “PtfmModel” should be selected so that “UserPtfmLd” subroutine will be called in the analysis. For FAST v7.01.00a-bjj, 16-Feb-2012 it can be any of the following options:

i. PtfmModel=1 and PtfmLdMod=1   
ii. PtfmModel=2 and PtfmLdMod=1   
iii. PtfmModel=3 and PtfmLdMod=1

This is necessary that the SACS supplied DLL is called (more details on this in the “Executable creation” section).

3. Invoke the 'SACS Non-Integrated FAST Analysis' sub analysis type under Utilities analysis type and set up the run. When requested for “Non-Integrated FAST Module”, the user should provide the executable (exe) for the FAST module. The exe provided should be compiled based on the instructions provided in the “Executable creation” section below.

Note: the executable can be located anywhere, but the following rules should be followed.

i. Preferred method: Place the FAST executable in the SACS system directory. This will allow the FAST executable to access the DLL (FAST_SACS_DLL.dll) and the static library (FAST_SACS_DLL.lib) directly.   
ii. Alternative method: The FAST executable can be located anywhere on the computer. In this case the user should copy and place the DLL from the SACS system folder to the same folder as the working directory. This may require the user to copy the license file Bentley.liclib.dll or Bentley.liclib.xx.dll (where xx is the version number) from the installation directory to the directory where the FAST exe is located.

4. The above run will create an OCI file containing the model definition and the generated inertial loads at each time increment. The OCI file can subsequently be used for a Fatigue or a Strength analysis using the procedure outlined for the integrated approach.

4.2.1.1 Executable Creation:

In order to create the executable so as to use the couple SACS FAST analysis the following two steps need to be taken.

1. Replace the “UserPtfmLd” subroutine in FAST with the one provided by SACS. This can be easily done by commenting out (or deleting) the subroutine from the FAST source files and adding file “SACS_Additions_n.f90” to the FAST project. The SACS_Additions_n.f90 subroutine is available under the SACS system directory.

Use “FAST_SACS_DLL.lib” as an additional dependency (or any other preferred method to use a static library) in the FAST project.

4.2.2 FAST MODULAR version 8.xx and newer

The SACS-FAST Non-Integrated (Modular) analysis workflow is the same as that for the older version (FAST 7.xx) except for the following differences:

1. The analysis should use the dynamic super element option for DynPac and Wave Response modules.

Enter “DSE” in columns 78-80 of the DYNOP2 line in DynPac input file

2. Create a Dynamic super element input file with option “F” in column 11, and option “FRC” in columns 28-30 of the DSEOPT line.   
3. Invoke the 'SACS Modular Non-Integrated FAST Analysis' sub analysis type under Utilities analysis type and set up the run. When requested for “Non-Integrated FAST Module”, the user should provide the executable (exe) for the FAST module. The exe provided should be compiled based on the instructions provided in the “Executable creation” section below.

Note: the executable can be located anywhere, but the following rules should be followed.

i. Preferred method: Place the FAST executable in the SACS system directory. This will allow the FAST executable to access the DLL

(SACS_FAST_Mod_DLL.dll) and the static library (SACS_FAST_Mod_DLL.lib) directly.

ii. Alternative method: The FAST executable can be located anywhere on the computer. In this case the user should copy and place the DLL from the SACS system folder to the same folder as the working directory. This may require the user to copy the license file Bentley.liclib.dll or Bentley.liclib.xx.dll (where xx is the version number) from the installation directory to the directory where the FAST exe is located.

4. The above run will create an OCI file containing the model definition and the generated inertial loads at each time increment. The OCI file can subsequently be used for a Fatigue or a Strength analysis using the procedure outlined for the integrated approach.

4.2.2.1 Executable Creation:

In order to create the executable so as to use the couple SACS FAST analysis the following two steps need to be taken.

1. Replace the “SubDyn” subroutine in FAST with the one provided by SACS. This can be easily done by Replacing the SACS provided SubDyn.f90 with the original from FAST. The SubDyn.f90 subroutine is available under the SACS system directory.

Use “SACS_FAST_Mod_DLL.lib” as an additional dependency (or any other preferred method to use a static library) in the FAST project.

## 4.3 DYNAMIC SUPER ELEMENT

The jacket structure can also be reduced to a dynamic super element using the SACS Dynamic Superelement module. The module allows the generation of a dynamic superelement based upon the Craig-Brampton approach. The generation of a dynamic superelement and the corresponding reduced load vector is a three step process. The first step is to run the SACS Dynpac module to produce mass, mode, the dynamic superelement data and transformation files. Next, the SACS Wave Response module is used to generate the dynamic superelement force file. Lastly, the SACS Dynamic Superelement module is used to generate the reduced stiffness, mass, damping and load vector.

NOTE: The wave response run can be omitted if the load vector is not required.

The above workflow is depicted in a graphical form below.

![](SACS2024_SACS_Documentation/chunk38_377fb3b9382aaf8633cdca8b6c86ece287faf142a98f34ea517cbce57b94feb5.jpg)

Full details on the generation of a Dynamic Super Element can be found in the Dynamic Superelement manual.

5 DAMAGE CALCULATION VERIFICATION

The fatigue damage is calculated in 3 phases as follows:

PHASE 1: Generation of Sacs Common Solution file

PHASE 2: Generation of damage files from each simulation

PHASE 3 Accumulation of Damage

The fatigue damage calculations are verified for Phases 2 and 3 mentioned above. The details are provided below:

## 5.1 GENERATION OF DAMAGE FILES FOR EACH SIMULATION

For generating the damage file for each simulation fatigue time history analysis is undertaken. This uses rainflow counting technique for different stress ranges and uses these to calculate the damage and thus the service life of the member. For validation purposes, the damage was calculated from stress cycles measured and compared with the calculations from SACS.

![](SACS2024_SACS_Documentation/chunk38_e10ffed55cc27edaddfd67e0a6339afb9fc5c2a41528a3f8d454bba1d695c105.jpg)

## 5.3 ACCUMULATION OF DAMAGE

The accumulation of damage phase needs to sum up the damage from all the common solution files (CSF’s). As mentioned above it happens in two stages. Firstly, the damage of 16 CSF’s is summed up in one run. Similar fatigue runs of 16 CSF summations are run in parallel (based on number of cores available). Thus for 100 CSF’s, there will be 6 such runs. Finally, the last run will sum up the damage calculated in these 6 runs (for 100 CSF case) and add it to the damage from the remaining 4 CSF’s

This verification is undertaken by using multiple copies of a single CSF file. Thus if we make 100 such copies, then the damage should be 100 times the damage of a single CSF file. For this verification, the CSF file chosen is the file used for validation of Phase 2. Thus we know that the damage for the single CSF is accurate.

A sample GH bladed process run was created with 100 cases. It can be seen that the fatigue damage (see listing file transcript below) for each run is 16 times the damage calculated in Phase 2. This is verified for all the runs in Folders 1 through 6.

![](SACS2024_SACS_Documentation/chunk38_2046baff8004642212acf4b4dce04301cf079fcf74daea7c00f535b963c87451.jpg)

Damage from 1 Fatigue run (16 CSF files)

Also the final summation run in the FTG folder (Ftglst.sum) reports the damage from the final summation for all 100 cases. It can be seen that the damage is 100 times the damage reported in Phase 2.

![](SACS2024_SACS_Documentation/chunk38_e2bdea923cb95ea91cc9e6d9e55b87978b2bbbb2a3602c26633b20ea5dd21c3d.jpg)
